raw_case_text:
We evaluated a 9-year-old boy from Onitsha, Nigeria, who presented with a 5-month history of left thigh swelling which progressively increased in size and became painful. He had had no preceding similar swelling or constitutional symptoms. However, about 2 months earlier, he was said to have been treated over a period of 1 month by a traditional bone setter for a presumed left femur fracture sustained in a pedestrian injury. Physical examination revealed a differentially warm, firm, slightly tender mass measuring about 6 cm x 4 cm in the anterolateral part of the distal left thigh. It was not attached to the overlying skin but partly fixed to the underlying structures, and the range of motion of the knee joint was reduced.
X-ray report showed a reduction in the corticomedullary differentiation of the distal metaphysis of the femur with soft-tissue swelling, preserved fat plane, spiculated periosteal reaction, cortical erosion, and cauterization [Figure 1]. Computed tomography (CT) scan report showed a reduced corticomedullary differentiation in the distal metaphysis of the femur with a sunray periosteal reaction with cortical erosion and a hypodense avascular soft-tissue mass in the distal femur [Figure 2]. Both X-ray and CT scan reports were in keeping with Ewing's sarcoma.
The patient was HIV negative and he had a packed cell volume of 35% and total white cell count of 11.4 x 109/l with differentials of 89% neutrophils and 11% lymphocytes. Intraoperative findings when an open biopsy was done included a fibrocystic mass containing brownish fluid situated on, but not attached to the anterolateral portion of the distal femur. Histology report from the biopsy showed numerous histiocytes and a few multinucleated giant cells. Many of the histiocytes have eccentrically located nuclei with cytoplasmic vacuoles containing figure-of-eight-shaped bodies. Similar bodies were also seen in the giant cells and also extracellularly [Figure 3]. The fungal bodies were also identified using periodic acid-Schiff-staining technique [Figure 4].
Postoperatively, he had a course of analgesics and antibiotics. When the lesion was confirmed to be of fungal origin, he was commenced on oral itraconazole (200 mg) daily. The surgical incision healed uneventfully, and the patient was discharged home 2 weeks later on oral itraconazole, which he took for a year. Follow-up in our hospital continued for the next 2 years and included clinical examination of the patient and x-rays of the affected femoral bone [Figure 5]. Subsequently, follow-up by telephone communication with the father was used to inquire if any swelling like the initial one treated has developed. There has been none.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy from Onitsha, Nigeria, presented with a 5-month history of a progressively enlarging, painful distal left thigh swelling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 5 months prior to evaluation, the child developed a gradually enlarging and increasingly painful mass on the anterolateral aspect of his distal left thigh. Approximately 2 months prior to presentation, he had been treated for 1 month by a traditional bone setter for a presumed left femoral fracture following a pedestrian road traffic injury.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pedestrian trauma with traditional bone setter manipulation 2 months prior; no prior medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful left thigh swelling and reduced left knee motion; negative for fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Local examination of the distal left thigh revealed a 6 x 4 cm differentially warm, firm, mildly tender mass over the anterolateral distal femur that was mobile under the skin but partially fixed to deep structures, with restricted left knee range of motion.
objective.routine_investigations: Packed cell volume (hematocrit) was 35%, WBC was 11.4 x 10^9/L (89% neutrophils, 11% lymphocytes), and HIV serology was negative. Left femur radiograph showed reduced corticomedullary differentiation in the distal femoral metaphysis, cortical erosion, spiculated periosteal reaction, and soft-tissue swelling.
objective.advanced_workup: Distal left femur CT demonstrated loss of metaphyseal corticomedullary differentiation, a 'sunray' spiculated periosteal reaction, cortical erosion, and a hypodense avascular soft-tissue mass radiologically mimicking Ewing sarcoma. Open excisional/incisional biopsy revealed a para-osseous fibrocystic mass containing brownish fluid; histopathology (H&E and periodic acid-Schiff stains) demonstrated numerous vacuolated histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells containing large thick-walled, figure-of-eight budding yeast cells diagnostic of Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: African histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum var. duboisii) of the distal left thigh and femur radiologically masquerading as Ewing sarcoma in an HIV-negative 9-year-old Nigerian boy, confirmed by open biopsy histopathology and PAS staining demonstrating characteristic intracellular and extracellular figure-of-eight budding yeast forms. Treated with surgical biopsy/debridement and a 1-year course of oral itraconazole (200 mg daily), achieving complete clinical and radiographic healing with no recurrence over 2+ years of follow-up.
